query: For additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy with an fcc matrix, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs degradation during elevated-temperature exposure to oxidizing or reducing gases and why catastrophic failure may occur? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, predicted observations relative to the starting-state baseline, applicable exposure boundaries, supporting prior evidence, and a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 high-entropy alloy (HEA) with an FCC matrix, degradation under elevated-temperature exposure is primarily driven by the formation of a non-adherent, porous oxide scale along grain boundaries. This scale, which forms due to accelerated cation and oxygen diffusion at high temperatures, leads to localized internal oxidation and microcrack formation. Once the oxide scale spalls, fresh surfaces are exposed, triggering a cascade of rapid degradation that can ultimately result in catastrophic failure.
generation.material_initial_state: An additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 HEA with a homogeneous FCC microstructure and minimal pre-existing defects.
generation.intervention: Switch the thermal treatment atmosphere between oxidizing (e.g., oxygen-rich air) and reducing (e.g., hydrogen-diluted environment) gases during high-temperature exposure.
generation.conditions: Elevated-temperature exposures in the range of 700°C to 900°C for durations up to 48 hours under controlled gas compositions.
generation.structural_mediator: Grain boundary regions and associated defect sites where the oxide scale nucleates and evolves.
generation.mechanism: At high temperatures, enhanced diffusivity allows selective cation migration and oxygen ingress along grain boundaries, leading to the nucleation and growth of an oxide layer. Under oxidizing conditions, the oxide layer thickens and becomes porous; successive growth and subsequent spallation expose fresh metal, creating stress concentrations and microcracks. Under reducing conditions, while a thinner scale may form, residual oxygen can still penetrate through microdefects, inducing internal oxidation. The accumulation of these defects undermines mechanical integrity and eventually triggers catastrophic failure.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under oxidizing gas exposure, there will be a rapid increase in weight gain due to oxide formation, the development of a thick but porous and spalling oxide scale along grain boundaries, and an elevated density of microcracks which will lead to reduced mechanical strength. In contrast, reducing atmospheres will slow the oxide growth rate; however, observable internal oxidation and subtle microstructural defects will still initiate degradation, albeit at a slower rate than in oxidizing conditions.
generation.baseline: The as-manufactured HEA in an inert or low-temperature environment exhibits a uniform, adherent surface without significant oxide scale or microcrack formation, maintaining its initial mechanical properties.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies specifically to service conditions where the alloy is exposed to atmospheres with well‐defined oxidizing or reducing potentials at temperatures between 700°C and 900°C. Outside these conditions, or if the alloy experiences alternate degradation pathways (e.g., due to mechanical overload or thermal cycling extremes), the governing mechanisms may differ.
generation.uncertainty: While the general role of oxide scale formation and spallation in promoting degradation is supported, the exact kinetics of diffusion, the influence of minor compositional fluctuations, and the transition thresholds between protective and destructive oxide behavior remain uncertain and require further investigation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare specimens of the additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy and subject them to high-temperature exposures (700°C and 900°C) in two controlled atmospheres: an oxidizing environment (oxygen-rich air) and a reducing environment (a hydrogen-diluted atmosphere). Monitor the progression of oxidation by periodic weight gain measurements and perform detailed microstructural analyses using SEM, TEM, and XRD after selected time intervals. Simultaneously, carry out mechanical testing (e.g., tensile or compression tests) to correlate degradation with reductions in material strength.
measurements: Weight gain and oxide scale thickness
Phase identification in the oxide scale and substrate
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no significant differences are observed in oxide scale characteristics (thickness, porosity, spallation) and associated microcrack densities between oxidizing and reducing conditions, and if mechanical properties remain largely unchanged relative to the inert baseline, then the hypothesis that oxide-scale evolution governs the degradation pathway and catastrophic failure is falsified.

Nanoscale origins of the damage tolerance of the high-entropy alloy CrMnFeCoNi

Abstract: AbstractDamage tolerance can be an elusive characteristic of structural materials requiring both high strength and ductility, properties that are often mutually exclusive. High-entropy alloys are of interest in this regard. Specifically, the single-phase CrMnFeCoNi alloy displays tensile strength levels of ∼1 GPa, excellent ductility (∼60–70%) and exceptional fracture toughness (KJIc>200 MPa√m). Here through the use of in situ straining in an aberration-corrected transmission electron microscope, we report on the salient atomistic to micro-scale mechanisms underlying the origin of these properties. High Temperature Oxidation Behavior of an Equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co High-Entropy Alloy

Abstract: AbstractThe oxidation behavior of an equimolar Cr-Mn-Fe-Co high-entropy alloy (HEA) processed by 3D laser printing was investigated at 700 °C and 900 °C. The oxidation kinetics of the alloy followed the parabolic rate law, and the oxidation rate constant increased with the rising of the temperature. Inward diffusion of oxygen and outward diffusion of cations took place during the high-temperature oxidation process. A spinel-type oxide was formed on the surface, and the thickness of the oxide layer increased with the rising of experimental temperature or time. The exfoliation of the oxide layer took place when the test was operated at 900 °C over 12 h. During oxidation tests, the matrix was propped open by oxides and was segmented into small pieces. The formation of loose structures had great effects on the high-temperature oxidation resistance of the HEA.Keywords: metals and alloys, 3D printing, oxidation
